doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Finding an angle and writing liner notes
summary: He looks at an artist's background, as in his Rene Rosnes piece, and wrote an honest liner note for a Mike Westbrook reissue.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: If you got an assignment to write about someone who has been written about a lot, could you envision how you would find your own angle to get at this person?

My own attitude or my own tendency is usually to look at the history. In other words I did a piece on the pianist Rene Rosnes not too long ago. Well I wanted to find out what made her tick. I didn’t actually want to do another puff about her latest record. What editors want often is just don’t talk to her about her record. You know that will please the record company. Well I’d much rather sort of find out what made her the pianist she is in terms of her influences, a little bit of her history and background, and maybe one or two of the, well incidents in her life. And that’s what I did. So I tend to want to find out about the jumping off point. What made a person become what they are? What was the kick start? That’s where I would tend to go. And also maybe to get a little something about the environment. Because America is such a range of fascinating contrasts. It’s (a) a polyglot population and community, and (b) there is such diverse differences, aren’t there? Because of the enormity of the country, because of the many strands of cultural change and variation, and it’s quite interesting to talk to people about that.
Did you ever get an assignment to write liner notes for a recording that you didn’t like?

I’m just trying to think. I don’t think so. Well I did do one recently for a Mike Westbrook reissue and I thought the music was pretty — well it left me fairly cold. I think you do as professional a job as you can. I sought to describe it. I sought to highlight what seemed to me to be the aspects that were valuable, and did it as honestly as I could. But of course the liner notes, as the late Stanley Dance put it, is a form of sales promotion, isn’t it? It’s unusual to start a liner and say this is unbelievably unpleasant music. So you have to find ways. That’s rare though.
